title: America's Chief Trade Negotiator Lands in India Tomorrow. The Deal Is 99 Percent Done.
excerpt: US Ambassador Sergio Gor says only the last 1 percent remains. A delegation arrives June 1 for four days of final talks that could seal the biggest bilateral trade pact in two decades.
body:
The United States and India are closer to a formal trade agreement than they have been at any point in the past two decades. US Ambassador Sergio Gor said on Friday that negotiations on an interim bilateral trade deal are 99 percent complete, and that the final text could be signed "over the next few weeks and months."

Speaking at the US-India TRUST Initiative — Transforming the Relationship Utilising Strategic Technologies — at the Indian Institute of Technology in New Delhi, Gor confirmed that an Indian delegation had travelled to Washington DC the previous week to resolve the last outstanding points. He said an American team, led by the country's chief trade negotiator, would arrive in New Delhi on June 1 for four days of talks to close the remaining gap.

"Our current interim trade agreement is on the table for us to finalise, and that will unlock prosperity for both of our countries," Gor said. "Just last week, India had sent a team to Washington DC to finalise the last one percent of that trade deal."

## What the Deal Covers

The interim agreement is designed to reduce tariffs and ease market access across several high-value sectors. US and Indian officials have identified pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, energy, critical minerals, and emerging technologies as the primary domains.

India supplies nearly 40 percent of generic medicines imported by the United States, and fresh investments are already flowing into the sector. Collaboration in semiconductors and cloud computing is expanding. Both nations are also increasing cooperation in strategic resources and energy security, with a new framework for critical minerals aligned to concerns over China's tightening grip on rare earth exports.

Bilateral trade between the two countries has grown from roughly $20 billion two decades ago to over $220 billion in goods and services today. The US is now one of India's largest trading partners, and India ranks among America's top trading partners.

## Why India Is Still Cautious

Despite Gor's optimism, India has signalled that it will not rush to sign until the broader US tariff landscape becomes clearer. The Trump administration imposed reciprocal tariffs of up to 50 percent on several categories of Indian goods in 2025, and while the current 90-day tariff pause has created space for negotiations, New Delhi wants certainty that the interim deal's terms will hold.

Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said India presents a "compelling case" for a bilateral agreement, citing the country's demographics, growth trajectory, and consumer market. But he has also cautioned that there is "no head-to-the-gun approach" — India's negotiators will prioritise national interests over deadlines.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the estimated 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, the deal could have direct implications. Pharma exports, IT services, and technology partnerships are sectors in which the Indian diaspora is heavily represented. Reduced trade barriers in advanced manufacturing and digital services could open new corridors for cross-border investment and entrepreneurship.

The agreement would also set a precedent. Gor pointed out that the EU and India have been negotiating a trade deal for almost 19 years without conclusion. If Washington and New Delhi close this interim pact within two years of starting talks, it would become the fastest major trade agreement India has concluded with a Western economy.

## What Happens Next

The US delegation led by the chief trade negotiator is expected in New Delhi from June 1 to 4. If the remaining issues — likely involving sensitive tariff lines, agricultural market access, and regulatory commitments — are resolved, both sides expect a signing ceremony in the coming weeks.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who recently concluded a four-day India visit, was also positive about the pact, saying the two sides would "wind up with a trade agreement" that is enduring and mutually beneficial.

The stakes are high. A successful deal would not only reshape the $220 billion trade corridor but also signal that the US-India strategic partnership is moving from rhetoric to binding economic architecture.
author: Diaspora Desk
